name: ישר ומישור במרחב – מצב הדדי, זווית ומרחק (באנגלית)
questiontext:
Different lines and planes in \(R^3\) admit a variety of mutual configurations. We can find all possibilities in this little figure as follows:

For a line and a plane there are three possibilities:

(1) The line \(n\) is parallel to the plane \(X\), (2) The line \(m\) intersects both planes \(X,Y\), (3) The line \(n\) is contained in the plane \(Y\).

For two planes there are again three possibilities:

(1) The planes \(X\) and \(Y\) are parallel, (2) The planes \(X\) and \(Z\) intersect in a line, (3) The plane \(X\) coincides with itself.

Consider the plane \(P: \left\{v \in R^3 \ | \ v \cdot {{CT:0}} = {{CT:1}} \right\} \) and the line \(\ell: {{CT:2}} + Span \left( {{CT:3}} \right) \)

a

Find a vector \(0 \ne n \in R^3\) normal to the plane \(P\). Namely a vector \(n\) such that \(n \cdot (w_1 - w_2) = 0, \ \forall w_1,w_2 \in P \). Make sure that you understand why this is what is required of a normal (=orthogonal) vector to the plane!

\(n\) = [[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]

How to enter: each entry in its own box: a number, a fraction (e.g. 1/2) or an expression (e.g. sqrt(2)).

b

What is the cosine of the angle between the direction of the line and the normal to the plane

\(cos(\angle(n, v)) = \) [[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans2]]
c

What is their mutual configuration (enter a number 1=parallel, 2=intersecting, 3=the line is contained in the plane):

[[input:ans3]]
[[validation:ans3]]
d

What is the distance between \(P\) and \(\ell\)

[[input:ans4]]
[[validation:ans4]]
generalfeedback:
Outline: Read the normal from the equation of the plane, compare it with the direction of the line (inner product), and use the result to decide the configuration and the distance.
Step 1 — A normal vector (part a)
The plane is the set of vectors \(v\) with \(v\cdot n=c\), where

\[ n={{CT:0}},\qquad c={{CT:1}} \]

If \(w_1,w_2\in P\), then \(n\cdot w_1=n\cdot w_2=c\), so \(n\cdot(w_1-w_2)=0\). Hence the coefficient vector \(n\) is normal to \(P\); any nonzero multiple of it is normal as well:

\[ n={{CT:0}} \]

Step 2 — The cosine of the angle (part b)
The direction of the line is \(v={{CT:3}}\). By the inner product formula:

\[ \cos(\angle(n,v))= rac{v\cdot n}{\|v\|\,\|n\|}= rac{{{CT:4}}}{[[if test="{{CT:14}}"]]{{CT:5}}[[else]]\sqrt{{{CT:6}}}[[/if]]\cdot[[if test="{{CT:15}}"]]{{CT:7}}[[else]]\sqrt{{{CT:8}}}[[/if]]}={{CT:9}} \]

Step 3 — The mutual configuration (part c)
The line is parallel to the plane or contained in it exactly when its direction is orthogonal to the normal, that is, when \(v\cdot n=0\). [[if test="{{CT:16}}"]]Here \(v\cdot n={{CT:4}} e 0\), so the line is not parallel to the plane and meets it in exactly one point: the configuration is

\[ 2\ ext{(intersecting)} \]

[[else]]Here \(v\cdot n=0\), so the line is parallel to the plane or contained in it. To decide, check whether the point \(w={{CT:2}}\) of the line lies in \(P\):

\[ n\cdot w={{CT:10}},\qquad c={{CT:1}} \]

[[if test="{{CT:17}}"]]The equation holds, so \(w\in P\) and the line is contained in the plane: the configuration is

\[ 3\ ext{(contained)} \]

[[else]]\(n\cdot w e c\), so \(w otin P\) and the line is parallel to the plane: the configuration is

\[ 1\ ext{(parallel)} \]

[[/if]][[/if]]
Step 4 — The distance (part d)
[[if test="{{CT:18}}"]]The line is parallel to the plane, so all its points are at the same distance from \(P\), and it is enough to take \(w\). The distance of \(w\) from the plane is the length of the projection of \(w-u\) on \(n\), for any point \(u\) of the plane; take \(u={{CT:11}}\), which satisfies \(u\cdot n={{CT:1}}\):

\[ d= rac{|(w-u)\cdot n|}{\|n\|}= rac{|{{CT:12}}|}{[[if test="{{CT:15}}"]]{{CT:7}}[[else]]\sqrt{{{CT:8}}}[[/if]]}={{CT:13}} \]

[[else]]The line and the plane have a common point, so the distance between them is

\[ d={{CT:13}} \]

[[/if]]

prts.name: prt1
prts.feedbackvariables: ngood: if (ans1 = zervect) then false else (if (crossprod(n,ans1)=zervect) then true else false);

on_true.feedback: Part a — correct. Yes the vector {@ans1@} is clearly normal (=orthogonal) to the plane \(P\) just by the equation defining this plane: \(v \cdot {{CT:0}} = {{CT:1}}\). Of course any nonzero scalar multiple of this vector is also good.
Part a — incorrect. The zero vector is clearly orthogonal to any plane. But you were asked for a non-zero vector.

on_false.feedback: Part a — incorrect. You chose a wrong normal (=orthogonal) vector. An obvious choice would have been the vector {{CT:19}} which is clearly normal to the plane \(P\) just by the equation defining this plane: \(v \cdot {{CT:0}} = {{CT:1}}\). Of course any nonzero scalar multiple of this vector would also work.

on_true.feedback: Part b — correct. You found the correct cosine of the angle between the line and the normal vector.
Part b — correct. You found the correct cosine of the angle between the line and the normal vector.

Part b — incorrect. This is the cosine of the angle between the direction of the line and the plane itself. You were asked to find the angle between the same direction and the normal vector \({{CT:0}}\) found in the previous question.

on_false.feedback:
Part b — incorrect. Sorry you got this angle wrong. You were asked to find the angle between the two vectors \(v={{CT:3}}\) and \(n={{CT:0}}\). This is readily given by the inner product as follows:

\[cos(\angle(v,n)) = \frac{v \cdot n}{||v|| ||n||} = \frac{{{CT:3}} \cdot {{CT:0}}}{\left|\left|{{CT:3}}\right|\right| \left|\left|{{CT:0}}\right|\right|} = {{CT:9}}.\]

on_true.feedback: Part c — correct. Yes, you found the correct mutual configuration of \(P\) and \(\ell\).

on_false.feedback: Part c — incorrect. No, you did not find the correct mutual configuration of \(P\) and \(\ell\).

on_true.feedback: Since \(n\) is not orthogonal to \(v\) we can immediately deduce that the line \(\ell\) intersects the plane \(P\) in one point. One can find this point by solving a system of equations but this is not necessary in order to solve the question.

on_false.feedback:
Since \(n\) is orthogonal to \(v\) we can immediately deduce that the line \(\ell\) is either contained or parallel to the plane \(P.\) In order to distinguish between these two possibilities it is enough to check if \(w \in P\). Of course any other point on the line could serve us just as well.
In order to determine if \(w \in P\) we just check if it satisfies the equation defining the plane

\[n \cdot w = {{CT:0}} \cdot {{CT:2}} = {{CT:10}}\]

on_true.feedback: Since the equation does not hold we deduce that the line \(\ell\) is parallel to the plane \(P\).

on_false.feedback: Since the equation is satisfied we deduce that the line \(\ell\) is contained in the plane \(P\)

on_true.feedback: Part d — correct. Yes, you calculated the distance correctly.

Since the line and the plane are parallel there is a positive distance between them. In order to find the distance between them let us first find a point on the plane. For example by solving the defining system of equations:

\[{@vec@} \cdot {{CT:0}} = {@vec.n@} = {{CT:1}}\]

One solution of this single equation with three unknowns (x,y,z) has many solutions. One of them for example is \(u = {{CT:11}}\).
Now we can find the distance by taking a vector \(w-u= {{CT:2}}-{{CT:11}} = {{CT:20}}\) and projecting it on the normal direction.

\[d = Proj_n(w-u) = \left| \left| \frac{(w-u) \cdot n}{n \cdot n} n \right| \right| = {{CT:13}}\]
Since the plane and the line intersect the distance between them is zero.

on_false.feedback: Since the line is contained in the plane the distance between them is zero.
